intro:
These exercises take the chapter's central claim seriously: verifiable LLM inference is an artifact pipeline before it is a model call, and Rust's job is to keep four boundaries honest. You separate verifier-visible claims from witness-only material, push heavyweight proving out of the request path, encode the public/private split into distinct types, and refuse to let preprocessing or serialization drift turn a protocol contract into an intermittent failure. The recurring discipline is ownership: who is allowed to hold the witness, who only ever sees the proof and the public claim, and which artifacts must be versioned even though they are not secret.

The lab and the profiling exercises ground the rest. They force you to treat GPU acceleration as a measured routing decision rather than a default, and to keep the verifier lane structurally witness-free so a leak becomes a compile error instead of an audit finding. By the end you should be able to look at any ZKML workflow and immediately sort every field into public, witness, or artifact-bound, and name the queue, lane, and version concerns that turn a prototype into something operable.

exerciseSolutions.title: Classify which parts of an LLM inference workflow are public, private, deterministic, or artifact-bound
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Start from the three questions the chapter uses to anchor every boundary: what is the verifier supposed to learn, what must the prover know, and what must both sides agree on in advance. Each field in the workflow falls into one of those buckets, and a field can be both public and artifact-bound at the same time.

Public inputs the verifier is expected to see: the public model hash, the verifier key ID, the output commitment, and the quantization bits. These are exactly the claim plus the proof-artifact references that the chapter's PublicClaim and ProofArtifact types carry. The verifier checks the proof against these and learns nothing else about the run. The quantization bits are public because they are part of the signed numeric contract, not because the value itself is sensitive.

Witness-only material that stays on the proving side: the prompt token IDs and the attention mask. These are the private execution trace. They are precisely what the chapter warns must never reach the verifier edge, because the entire point of the proof is to let the verifier check the computation without seeing the private inputs. The proof blob is the artifact that lets the verifier do that check; it is verifier-facing, not witness.

Artifact-bound fields that must be versioned even when not secret: the tokenizer version, the model hash, the verifier key ID, and the quantization bits. Artifact-bound does not mean secret here; it means attributable and versioned so a mixed deployment can be diagnosed. The reproducibility consequence of misclassifying these is concrete: tokenization, quantization, and public-input ordering must all be deterministic and pinned, because if one deployment's tokenizer or quantization policy drifts from another's, the prover and verifier are reasoning about different graphs and cross-service verification fails intermittently with no obvious cause. That is a protocol break disguised as a flaky test.
criteria: Public claims (model hash, verifier key ID, output commitment, quantization bits) are kept distinct from witness material (prompt token IDs, attention mask).
At least two artifact-bound fields are named: model hash, verifier key ID, tokenizer version, and quantization bits.
A reproducibility consequence is named: drifted tokenization or quantization makes prover and verifier compute different graphs, causing intermittent cross-service verification failure.

exerciseSolutions.title: Design a Rust service boundary around an EZKL-style proving job
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The starting service does everything inline in one request handler: tokenize, build witness, prove, verify, and then store prompt text alongside the proof in a single response record. That collapses all four boundaries the chapter asks you to keep separate, and it leaks witness material into the stored record. Read it as four lanes that got flattened into one.

Which steps belong where: the submitter edge should accept the request, validate it, look up the artifact manifest (model hash, circuit ID, quantization and tokenizer versions, verifier key ID), enqueue a proving job, and return a receipt. Tokenization, witness generation, and proof generation belong in a proving worker lane behind that queue, because they are the heavyweight stages and they are the only stages that ever touch the witness. Verification is light and can live on its own thin verifier lane that consumes only the public claim plus a proof reference. The proving lane should look like a worker boundary, not a convenience helper called from the handler.

Which boundary first owns a manifest, and what must never appear on the verifier side: the submitter edge is where artifact-manifest lookup belongs, so version identity is resolved once and attached to the job rather than recomputed from request-local state in each stage. The verifier-facing request type must never carry prompt tokens, attention masks, or witness paths. In the broken service those are exactly the fields that ended up stored next to the proof; if the verifier request can see them, the boundary is already too wide and the proof's privacy promise is void.

Which metric exposes the inline pain: the inline design serializes proving inside the request, so the signal is request-handler latency and its tail, driven by proof generation time. The repaired design should expose queue age (how long a job waits before a worker picks it up) and per-stage timing for witness, prove, transfer, and verify, so you can see queue-bound versus prove-bound behavior instead of one opaque p99. Rising queue age under load is the honest indicator that proving must be bounded and backpressured rather than run inline.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The edge resolves the manifest and enqueues; the verifier type cannot name a witness field.
criteria: Tokenization, witness generation, and proof generation are moved out of the request handler into a worker lane behind a queue.
The verifier lane (VerificationRequest) is witness-free: it carries only the public claim and a proof reference.
Artifact-manifest lookup is placed explicitly at the submitter edge so version identity is resolved once.
Queue age and per-stage timing are named as the signals the repaired design should expose.

exerciseSolutions.title: Implement separate proving and verification request types
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The design goal is structural separation: the proving side must be the only side that can name witness material, and the verification side must be expressible using nothing but public claims and proof-artifact references. The chapter's verification-boundary example is the template. If one struct could serve both jobs, the boundary would still be vague, so the answer deliberately uses three distinct types plus a separate artifact type.

ProvingJob owns the witness fields (prompt tokens and attention mask) because the witness is born in the prover lane. ProofArtifact carries the proof-identity fields: the proof bytes, the circuit ID, and the verifier key ID. VerificationJob is built only from a public claim and a ProofArtifact reference; it has no field that can hold witness data, so a leak would require adding a field and would be visible in review. This is the type-level enforcement the chapter calls the cheapest enforcement you will ever get.

Versioning is in the shape from the start, not bolted on after a migration. The model_id carries a version tag, and circuit_id and verifier_key_id are explicit named identifiers rather than substrings of a path. Naming the circuit and verifier key as their own fields is what makes mixed deployments and failures attributable: when a verification fails across services, you can point at the exact circuit and key in play rather than parsing a file path. The design is small enough to review in one sitting, which is itself part of the acceptance bar.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Three distinct types: only ProvingJob can hold witness data; VerificationJob carries claim plus proof.
criteria: Proving and verification types are structurally distinct: ProvingJob, ProofArtifact, and VerificationJob are separate.
VerificationJob has no witness field, so it cannot require witness-only data.
Version and artifact identity are explicit: model_id is version-tagged, circuit_id and verifier_key_id are named fields.
The design is three small types reviewable at a glance.

exerciseSolutions.title: Repair numerical reproducibility drift before the prover and verifier split across services
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The failure is contract drift, which the chapter names as the most expensive ZKML mistake. Three independent changes each altered part of the signed contract: one deployment changed quantization bits, another changed tokenizer special-token handling, and a third reordered public inputs in a manifest serializer. None of these is a backend bug. Each one changes what graph or what public-input vector the two sides are reasoning about, so the proof no longer corresponds to the statement the verifier checks. Intermittent failure is the signature: it fails only when a request happens to route across two deployments that disagree.

What needs canonical ordering or stable layout: the public-input vector and the manifest serialization. Reordering public inputs changes the statement even when every value is identical, so the serializer must emit fields in a canonical, stable order with a fixed layout. That is the canonical-serialization repair. Separately, the preprocessing-version repair: tokenizer special-token handling and quantization bits must be pinned and versioned, because both are part of the numeric and tokenization contract the proof system signs, not free model-tuning knobs.

Why this is a protocol-compatibility bug and not just a runtime bug: a proof asserts that the chosen computation was followed over the chosen public inputs under the chosen assumptions. Quantization bits and tokenizer behavior determine the chosen computation and inputs. Change either and the prover proves a different statement than the verifier checks; the cryptography is working correctly and still reports a mismatch. So the right fix lives in the artifact manifest, not the proof engine.

The manifest should carry the model hash, circuit ID, quantization bits, tokenizer version, public-input layout version, and verifier key ID, so a mismatch is visible before any prove or verify runs. The CI gate is a contract test that fails the rollout when any deployment's manifest diverges: a golden-manifest comparison plus a canonicalization round-trip test that asserts the public-input serializer produces a fixed byte layout. That gate fires before rollout instead of leaving the break to surface as flaky cross-service verification.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: A versioned manifest plus an order-stable serializer turns drift into a pre-rollout contract failure.
criteria: One canonical-serialization repair (stable public-input ordering via order-stable layout) and one preprocessing-version repair (pinned, versioned quantization and tokenizer) are identified.
The issue is explained as a protocol-compatibility bug: the two sides prove and check different statements even though the proof backend is correct.
A CI/contract gate is proposed: golden-manifest comparison plus a canonicalization round-trip test that fails before rollout.

exerciseSolutions.title: Profile a hypothetical GPU-backed ZKML pipeline and identify the real bottleneck
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Keep the buckets separate, as the chapter insists: queue wait 700 ms, witness 260 ms, prove 1100 ms, verify 35 ms, transfer 220 ms. Proof generation at 1100 ms dominates wall time, with queue wait second at 700 ms. So the pipeline is prove-bound first and queue-bound second; it is not transfer-bound or verify-bound.

Which rewrite is premature: optimizing GPU transfer (220 ms) or verification (35 ms) is the wrong target. They are small relative to prove time, and shaving them cannot move the user-visible story while a 1100 ms prove stage stands. Equally, witness generation at 260 ms is not the lead suspect here, even though the chapter notes it can sometimes outweigh the prover. Measure, do not assume; in this window the data says prove dominates.

The next measurement inside the dominant category: break the 1100 ms prove stage into its internal phases for this proof backend and batch shape, for example setup or key load versus the actual proving rounds, and check how prove time scales with batch size and sequence length, since attention makes proving cost scale brutally with sequence length. That tells you whether the win is a different batch size, a different lane, or a backend change, rather than guessing.

Validation that the repair moved the real bottleneck and not a micro-metric: after a change, prove time should fall and the new dominant stage should be identified from the same five buckets, while end-to-end p50 and p95 improve and queue age does not silently grow to absorb the slack. If prove time drops but queue wait rises to keep total latency flat, you moved a micro-metric, not the bottleneck. Treat the GPU as workload-dependent: the right lane can flip between CPU-favorable and GPU-favorable as batch size, witness shape, and transfer cost change, so re-measure the dominant stage after any routing change rather than assuming the GPU helped.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Bucketed timing names prove as the dominant stage; transfer and verify are premature targets.
criteria: The dominant latency layer is identified correctly as proof generation (1100 ms), with queue wait (700 ms) second.
A wrong target is rejected: optimizing GPU transfer or verification cannot move wall time while prove dominates.

A deeper measurement (decompose prove time by phase and by batch/sequence scaling) and before/after metrics (prove time down, end-to-end p50/p95, new dominant stage, queue age not growing) are proposed.
GPU usage is treated as workload-dependent and re-measured rather than assumed correct.

exerciseSolutions.title: Productize ZKML with APIs, job orchestration, artifact versioning, and observability
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The design follows the chapter's product shape: submit, status, and verify behave like a job system with receipts, proving is heavy and bounded, verification is light, and every artifact is attributable. Mixed model versions and canary rollout are assumed, so version lookup is a first-class service concern rather than an afterthought.

Every artifact is content-addressed or versioned with an explicit custody rule. The model hash is content-addressed by hash, immutable, and the root of attribution. The circuit ID is versioned, pinned per model release, and immutable once published. The quantization manifest is versioned because it is part of the signed numeric contract, and changing it forks that contract; the tokenizer manifest is versioned for the same reason on the LLM side. The verifier key ID is versioned, paired with a specific circuit, and rotated deliberately, while the proof blob is content-addressed by digest, immutable, and referenced by status and verify but never regenerated silently. The witness ties this together by its absence: it is never an artifact in the registry, it stays in proving-side custody, and it is discarded once the proof is produced.

The CPU proving lane and the GPU proving lane get separate worker pools and separate queue budgets, because they have different capacity and failure profiles and you do not want GPU saturation to starve CPU jobs or vice versa. Verification gets its own lightweight pool since it is cheap and latency-sensitive, and it must not share a budget with proving. Fallback from GPU to CPU happens at the routing boundary: if the GPU lane is unavailable, saturated past its queue budget, or a job errors in a retryable way, the job is re-routed to the CPU lane rather than failing the request. That fallback is exposed to operators as an explicit fallback_rate metric and a per-job route field in the trace, so a silent collapse onto CPU, which would quietly raise latency, is visible rather than hidden inside business logic.

Before the service is production-ready, the observability surface needs queue age per lane for the load and backpressure signal, per-stage timing for witness, prove, transfer, and verify, proof bytes per job as a size and cost signal, verification failure rate as the correctness and drift signal, the GPU-to-CPU fallback rate, and the resolved artifact-version set per job in traces so a failure is attributable to a specific model hash, circuit, and verifier key. Alerts fire on rising queue age, rising verification failures, which often signals contract drift, and a fallback-rate spike. That combination makes proving heavy, verification light, and artifacts attributable, which is the bar the chapter sets.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Versioned registry, observable GPU-to-CPU fallback, and a per-job metrics record with attributable versions.
criteria: At least three artifacts are named with a custody/version rule each: model hash (content-addressed), circuit ID (versioned), quantization and tokenizer manifests (versioned contract), verifier key ID (versioned), proof blob (content-addressed); witness stays in proving-side custody.
Separate queue/worker budgets are defined for the CPU and GPU proving lanes (and a separate verification pool).
GPU-to-CPU fallback is an explicit routing rule with operator-visible fallback_rate, isolating GPU failure.
At least three observability hooks are named: queue age, per-stage timing, proof bytes, verification failure rate, fallback rate, and per-job artifact-version set.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
prove queue = zkml.gpu
verify payload = 2
witness leaked = false
labSolution.explanation:
The starter code's build_verification_job had three boundary defects: it copied the witness_path into the proof_path field (leaking a witness reference into the verifier lane), set public_output_count to a hardcoded 0 instead of counting the real public claims, and set witness_included to true. The fix makes the verifier lane witness-free. proof_path is sourced from job.proof_path so the verification job references the proof artifact, not the witness. public_output_count is computed as job.public_outputs.len(), which is 2 for token_hash and score_hash. witness_included is set to false because no witness material crosses into the verification request; model_id and witness_path remain in proving-side custody.

In main, prove_queue is chosen by the gpu_requested flag, which is true, so the route is zkml.gpu. The program then prints the queue, the public output count from the verification job, and the witness_included flag.

The output therefore reads: prove queue = zkml.gpu, verify payload = 2, and witness leaked = false. This is the chapter's boundary-honesty lesson made concrete: the verifier-facing request carries the public claim and a proof reference only, and witness material stays where it was generated.

For a real, GPU-runnable version of this idea, see public/ezkl-gpu/: it runs the model inference on the GPU via ONNX Runtime CUDA EP and then generates and verifies a genuine EZKL zero-knowledge proof of the model.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should verification requests usually stay witness-free?
reviewAnswers.answer: The whole point of verifiable inference is to let a third party check that a specific computation ran over the public inputs without seeing the private data, so the witness, the private execution trace, must never appear on the verifier edge. A verification request needs only the public claim and a reference to the proof artifact; the proof itself is what stands in for the witness. If prompt tokens, attention masks, or witness paths leak into the verification type, the privacy guarantee is void and the boundary has already widened too far. Keeping the verifier type structurally incapable of holding witness fields turns a potential leak into a compile error rather than an audit finding.

reviewAnswers.question: What makes tokenization, quantization, and public-input ordering protocol concerns instead of private implementation details?
reviewAnswers.answer: A proof asserts that the chosen computation was followed over the chosen public inputs under the chosen assumptions, and tokenization, quantization, and public-input ordering all determine what that chosen computation and input vector actually are. Change the tokenizer's special-token handling, the quantization bits, or the order of public inputs in the serializer, and the prover proves a different statement than the verifier checks, even though every value looks the same and the proof backend is working correctly. Because both sides must agree on these in advance, they belong in a versioned, signed artifact contract rather than in private, freely changeable implementation code. Treating them as tuning knobs instead of protocol fields is the contract drift the chapter calls the most expensive ZKML mistake.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is a proving lane usually a queue and capacity problem as much as a cryptography problem?
reviewAnswers.answer: Proving is the heavyweight stage, often dominating wall time, and under load the time a job spends waiting in the queue can dwarf the proving itself, so end-to-end latency is governed by queue age and worker capacity as much as by kernel speed. Running proving inline in a request handler serializes that cost into request latency and its tail, which is why the work belongs behind a bounded queue with its own worker pool. The right fixes are frequently operational, more workers, backpressure, separate CPU and GPU lane budgets, rather than a faster proof engine. Measuring queue wait separately from witness, prove, transfer, and verify is what reveals whether the lane is queue-bound or prove-bound.

reviewAnswers.question: What does a verifiable inference system prove, and what does it not prove?
reviewAnswers.answer: A passing proof says that the chosen computation was followed over the chosen public inputs under the chosen proving assumptions and artifacts, that is, that this specific frozen model graph, with these public inputs, produced the committed output. It does not prove that the model is truthful, fair, safe, aligned, or even useful; a perfectly valid proof can wrap a terrible answer. It also says nothing about whether the chosen artifacts were the right ones, only that they were the ones actually used. The guarantee is about computational integrity under a fixed contract, not about the quality or correctness of the model's behavior.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should GPU-backed proving still be treated as an optional execution lane rather than as the whole architecture?
reviewAnswers.answer: GPU performance in ZKML is workload-dependent: the same proof backend can shift from CPU-favorable to GPU-favorable and back as batch size, witness shape, and artifact transfer cost change, so the GPU is not automatically faster. The proving kernel is only one slice of wall time, and host-to-device copies, queue wait, or artifact staging can erase any kernel win, which is why every claim of GPU acceleration has to be earned with a measurement. Treating GPU as one routing policy, with explicit and observable fallback to a CPU lane, keeps the system honest and resilient when the GPU lane is saturated or unavailable. Building the architecture around the GPU instead hides a load-bearing assumption that the measurements may not support.
